title: Early Predatory Dinosaurs Endured Ecosystem Shift, New Fossil Fragment Reveals Survival Tactics
body:
A fragmentary femur unearthed in the Late Triassic rocks of southern Brazil has upended long‑standing assumptions about the fate of early predatory dinosaurs, showing that herrerasaurids—some of the first large, meat‑eating dinosaurs—survived well beyond the dramatic ecological turnover that reshaped their world around 225 million years ago.

The bone, recovered from the Candelária Formation of the Paraná Basin, bears diagnostic features that link it unmistakably to the herrerasaurid lineage, a group previously thought to have vanished shortly after the end‑Triassic mass extinction that wiped out many contemporary archosaurs. Radiometric dating places the stratum at roughly 215 million years old, a full ten million years after the last confirmed herrerasaurid fossils from Argentina’s Ischigualasto and Los Colorados formations. This temporal extension suggests that these early theropods were far more resilient than their fossil record implied, persisting alongside a rapidly evolving assemblage of sauropodomorphs, crocodylomorphs, and early mammals.

The discovery carries weighty implications for our understanding of Triassic ecosystems. The Late Triassic was a period of intense competition among archosaurs, with the rise of more derived theropods and the diversification of herbivorous sauropodomorphs reshaping predator–prey dynamics. Herrerasaurids, with their relatively primitive skeletal anatomy—short, robust forelimbs and a distinctive hip structure—were once considered ecological dead‑ends, outcompeted by faster, more efficient hunters. Yet the Brazilian femur indicates that at least some members of this group adapted to shifting prey availability, possibly exploiting niche habitats such as floodplain forests that were less accessible to larger carnivores.

Paleontologists caution that a single bone cannot reconstruct the full picture of herrerasaurid biology, but it does open new lines of inquiry. Dr. Mariana Lúcio, lead researcher on the project, notes that “the morphology of the femur suggests a sturdy, perhaps slower‑moving predator that could have relied on ambush tactics rather than pursuit.” If herrerasaurids occupied such a niche, they might have coexisted with emerging theropods by targeting different prey sizes or hunting at different times of day. Further fieldwork in the Paraná Basin may reveal additional remains—teeth, vertebrae, or even partial skeletons—that could clarify whether this survival was an isolated case or part of a broader, previously undocumented herrerasaurid population.

The find also prompts a re‑evaluation of the fossil record’s completeness. The scarcity of herrerasaurid specimens has long been attributed to their limited geographic range, but the new evidence suggests that sampling bias and taphonomic processes may have concealed a more extensive distribution across Gondwana. Brazil’s Triassic deposits have been less intensively explored than Argentina’s, and the discovery underscores the importance of expanding paleontological surveys in under‑studied regions. As more sites are investigated, scientists anticipate that other “missing” lineages could emerge, reshaping the evolutionary narrative of early dinosaurs.

Looking ahead, the Brazilian femur serves as a reminder that the early Mesozoic was a dynamic arena where evolutionary experiments unfolded in rapid succession. Ongoing excavations, combined with advances in geochronology and biomechanical modeling, will likely refine our picture of how primitive predators navigated the turbulent ecosystems of the Triassic. If herrerasaurids indeed persisted longer than previously thought, their eventual disappearance may have set the stage for the rise of the classic theropod clades that dominated the Jurassic and Cretaceous, highlighting a pivotal, albeit fleeting, chapter in the story of dinosaur evolution.
